title: How do you secure a microservices architecture (authentication/authorization, API gateway, TLS, service mesh, secrets management, RBAC)?
shortTitle: How do you secure a microservices architecture
keyPoints: Defence in depth: no single security control is enough; layer authentication, authorization, encryption, and secrets management.
Authentication with OAuth2 and JWT: a central identity provider issues signed tokens that each service validates locally.
Authorization with RBAC: roles ride inside the JWT as claims, and services enforce with @PreAuthorize annotations.
The API gateway terminates TLS, validates the JWT once, and applies rate limiting at the edge.
Mutual TLS (mTLS) encrypts service-to-service traffic and proves both caller and callee identity.
Secrets management via HashiCorp Vault or cloud secrets managers keeps credentials out of code.
Zero Trust: no request is trusted just because it came from inside the network; every service authenticates every request.

s1_definition.oneliner: Secure microservices with defence in depth: authenticate with OAuth2 and JWT, authorize with RBAC, terminate TLS at the gateway, encrypt service-to-service with mTLS, keep secrets in a vault, and trust nothing merely for being inside the network.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Authentication** – Establishes who the caller is, typically with OAuth2 and JWT bearer tokens validated locally by each service.
- **Authorization** – Decides what the caller may do, using role-based access control (RBAC) with roles carried as JWT claims.
- **API Gateway** – The single front door that terminates TLS, validates tokens, enforces rate limits, and routes requests.
- **Mutual TLS (mTLS)** – Both caller and callee present certificates so each proves its identity, preventing internal impersonation.
- **Secrets management** – Credentials stored encrypted in a system like HashiCorp Vault, rotated automatically, never in code.
- **Zero Trust** – No request is trusted merely because it originated inside the perimeter; every service verifies every request.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's headquarters. At the main entrance a guard checks every visitor's ID badge (authentication at the gateway). Each department door only opens for badges with the right clearance (role-based authorization). All internal mail is in sealed envelopes (TLS and mTLS). The master keys are in a locked cabinet that logs every access (secrets management). And nobody is trusted just because they are inside the building; every door still checks the badge (zero trust).

sections.s6_takeaway:
Securing a microservices architecture requires defence in depth across multiple layers. Authentication with OAuth2 and JWT establishes the caller's identity through a signed token each service validates locally. Authorization with RBAC maps users to roles carried as JWT claims, enforced with annotations like `@PreAuthorize`. The API gateway terminates TLS, validates the JWT once, and rate-limits at the edge.

Internally, mutual TLS ensures both caller and callee prove their identity with certificates, so an attacker inside the network cannot impersonate a service. A service mesh like Istio automates mTLS and authorization policies without changing application code. Secrets management via Vault keeps database passwords and API keys out of code, encrypted, access-controlled, and automatically rotated.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj configured the mobile app to call through the gateway, which validated the JWT and rate-limited. Each service still validated the token (zero trust) and ran its own RBAC check: a support agent could view accounts but was denied transfers because the SUPPORT role lacked the TRANSFER permission. When an attacker tried to call the transfer service directly with a forged token, mTLS rejected the connection before the token was even checked.

Remember one sentence: secure microservices with defence in depth: authenticate with OAuth2 and JWT, authorize with RBAC, terminate TLS at the gateway, encrypt service-to-service with mTLS, keep secrets in a vault, and trust nothing merely for being inside the network.
